create.title: Encrypt message
create.inputReadReceiptLabel: Read receipt (track when the secret is opened)
create.subtitle: Encrypted locally in your browser. Server only sees ciphertext. Key never leaves your device.
create.infoA1Body:
The key is a random 24-character string generated in your browser (AES-256 strength). It never appears in any network request — browsers transmit it via the URL # fragment, and HTTP guarantees fragments never reach the server (RFC 3986 §3.5).

Just share the full link with the recipient; their browser decrypts with the same key. The server has no key — it cannot decrypt.
create.infoA2Title: Why is sending only the ciphertext safe?
create.infoA2Body:
The ciphertext is the plaintext after OpenPGP encryption. Without the key, ciphertext is just random bytes. The server receives the ciphertext but has no key, so it cannot recover the plaintext.

This differs from ordinary HTTPS: HTTPS only protects transit (server can still read plaintext). Here the server never sees plaintext at all — true end-to-end encryption.
create.infoA3Body:
When checked, the ciphertext can only be decrypted once: after the first decryption the server deletes it and the link stops working.

Note: ① Refreshing the page counts as a new open and triggers the burn. ② Copying plaintext elsewhere is outside our control. ③ This is "burn after reading", not "auto-vanish" — save the plaintext immediately.
create.infoA4Body:
We recommend the default random key — generated by crypto.getRandomValues() with 24 chars of entropy, far beyond human memorability.

Use a custom key (uncheck this and type) when: ① you want to remember a passphrase yourself; ② you reuse a familiar phrase. Short keys are stretched via argon2, but weak keys reduce real-world security.
create.infoA5Body:
Countdown starts the moment you click "Generate one-time share link" — not when the recipient first opens it.

Example: pick 1 hour → the link expires 1 hour after creation, regardless of whether it's been opened. Pick 1 day if you want a 24-hour window for the recipient.
create.infoA6Title: What does the link look like?
create.infoA6Body:
A complete link looks like:

  https://one-pass.ohoooho.com/s/abc123#Y6d7737DKcgo2jU4YvE4s7

- /s/abc123 — where the ciphertext is stored on one-pass
- #Y6d7737DKcgo2jU4YvE4s7 — the key at the end of the URL

Just send the whole link. For better security, send the link and the key via separate channels (link via IM, key via phone call) to reduce interception risk.

features.title: Share secrets securely with ease
features.subtitle: Yopass is created to reduce the amount of clear text passwords stored in email and chat conversations by encrypting and generating a short lived link which can only be viewed once.
features.featureEndToEndText: Encryption and decryption are being made locally in the browser. The key is never stored with yopass.
features.featureSelfDestructionText: Encrypted messages have a fixed lifetime and will be deleted automatically after expiration.
features.featureOneTimeText: The encrypted message can only be downloaded once which reduces the risk of someone peeking at your secrets.
features.featureSimpleSharingText: Yopass generates a unique one click link for the encrypted file or message. The decryption password can alternatively be sent separately.
features.featureNoAccountsText: Sharing should be quick and easy; No additional information except the encrypted secret is stored in the database.
features.featureOpenSourceText: Yopass encryption mechanism are built on open source software meaning full transparency with the possibility to audit and submit features.

about.tagline: The server cannot see your plaintext. Your browser is the only place that encrypts.
about.insecureFlow: plaintext -> server encrypts -> store ciphertext -> client decrypts
about.secureFlow: browser generates key -> browser encrypts -> only ciphertext sent to server
about.secureRisk: Risk: server only sees ciphertext, cannot decrypt without key
about.evidenceTitle: Hard evidence the server cannot see the key
about.evidence1Body: URL fragments after # are NEVER sent to the server (RFC 3986 sec 3.5). Decryption keys live after #, so the browser never sends them.
about.evidence2Body: onepass-server only parses the URL path, never reads fragments (see pkg/server/server.go).
about.evidence3Body: On 140.143.246.15: tcpdump on the server port. You will NEVER see anything after #.
about.evidence4Body: Open https://one-pass.ohoooho.com/ -> F12 -> Network -> create a secret -> POST body only contains BEGIN PGP MESSAGE ciphertext. Plaintext never appears in any request.
about.risk1: Server sees metadata: IP, time, ciphertext size. We do not log IPs, but you should know this is an inherent HTTP limitation.
about.risk2: If you send the link to the wrong person, they have the key and can decrypt. Use a separate channel to send the key.
about.risk3: memcached restart -> links expire (by design: burn-after-reading). If your link returns 404, this is why.
about.promise1: Server logs only store UUIDs, never IP / UA.
about.promise4: Full source code Apache-2.0 open-source. Repository:
about.greenCaption: Only this is sent to the server (OpenPGP encrypted, no key = no decrypt)
about.redCaption: This key NEVER reaches the server (HTTP guarantees # is not transmitted)
about.serverNeverSees: The server never sees anything outside this box
